cultivar: Zhenghe Da Bai Cha (政和大白茶)
processing: One bud with one or two leaves, withered and dried without firing or rolling. Zhenghe lots are commonly withered longer than Fuding ones, which gives a little more oxidation and a heavier cup.
harvest_season: Spring, picked after the silver needle buds as the shoots open into a bud and one or two leaves.
appearance_dry: Loose mix of downy silver buds and darker olive-green leaves, leafy and open.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow, a shade deeper than a fresh Fuding peony.
appearance_wet: Bud and leaf sets in soft green with some reddish-brown edges.
taste_profile: Herbaceous and grainy with cream and nut, soft and malty-sweet in the mouth, with a stronger and longer finish than Fuding peony.

brewing.notes: Leafier than silver needle, so it takes hotter water. A long steep in a mug also works, since it rarely turns harsh.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, typically spring of the current year or kept and sold with some age; pressed cakes also exist in the wider Bai Mu Dan market. Sellers often state the vintage as a season and year, and that is the thing to ask for along with the cultivar.
description:
Bai Mu Dan means white peony, and it is the bud-and-leaf grade of white tea, picked after the pure buds of silver needle. This one comes from Zhenghe in northern Fujian and is made from the local Zhenghe Da Bai Cha plant, one of the two classic white tea cultivars alongside Fuding Da Bai.

Nothing is fired or rolled, but the wither is usually longer than in Fuding. That longer wither, on a thicker leaf, is why Zhenghe peony tends to read as more oxidised and heavier in the cup.

One tasted 2020 spring lot was described with cooked grain, new shoots, cream, nuts and a slight touch of tobacco, with a soft malty sweetness. That is a fair picture of the style: more herb and grain than flower. A 2022 comparison of Zhenghe white teas with Yunnan ones described the Zhenghe group as sweet and smooth. Hot water and a few medium steeps show it best.

It is less often sold under its origin name than Fuding is, so ask about the place and the plant. If you find Fuding peony too delicate, this is the natural next pot.
history: Bai Mu Dan as a style is generally dated to Fujian in the nineteenth century, though accounts differ on the exact timing for Zhenghe, and exact years should be taken with caution. Little independent documentation of how this tea developed in Zhenghe itself is easily available.
